That's the problem, they didn't market it really well. Initially it was meant as a console killer, steamOS is free which eliminates the need to drop $120 bucks on a Windows license, saving money on a mid-range system build and eliminating all of the windows overhead for better performance, and it links direct to Steam eliminating Windows Store. So it makes sense for Valve, take an existing and robust open source OS and skin it for gaming machines.

They just didn't support it very well... the Steam Machines released and nobody cared, there still isn't enough native Linux support from the devs.

I love talking about Steam Machines & SteamOS, but invariably people start taking offense because they conflate all criticism of SteamOS with a criticism of Linux (and sometimes they DO overlap). The only problems Steam Machines address is a business problem for Valve--i.e. as a hedge against Microsoft. Other than that, they just can't compete as a console killer. The main reason for this is that consoles are subsidized by Sony and Microsoft--they're sold at a big loss who make up money on the backend when you buy games. That model doesn't work for Steam Machines since they're made by 3rd-party partners who HAVE to make a profit. Right now you can grab a new Xbox One for well under $300 while decent Steam Machines retail at over $700. That's a game-over scenario (just ask 3DO).

And to be honest, SteamOS has never been ready for Prime Time. You and I have both struggled to do some basic stuff like get drivers working...and this invariably requires running Terminal commands. Console gamers ain't gonna play that shit, and neither will PC gamers--those guys don't know (and don't want to learn) basic Linux stuff--they just want to play games. I'm hesitant to even mention the fact that currently most modern games run worse on Linux so any hypothetical advantage that Valve touts for SteamOS/Linux is undermined in real world benchmarks. As long as that is the case, you're not going to interest the extreme-gamers who'll chase benchmarks even if it means leaving Windows.

That pretty much just leaves folks who already use Linux as an audience. Sure, there will be SOME folks (like you and me) who give SteamOS a try, but at the end of the day, why not just use a full featured distro and go Big Picture Mode within the Steam client? Or hook up an old laptop to your TV and stream it from a gaming rig (or just buy a Steam Link for $50).

Steam Machines and SteamOS just seem like pure folly. Valve's efforts would have been better invested in integrating the Steam client in major distros.

Is kinguin a legit reseller? I know a lot of sites rip off the developers and don't pay them.

Here's an article that explains it better than I can.

The bottom line is that yes, the codes are legit. They come from all over--some result from sales, some come from other countries where prices are lower, some (probably the Windows licenses) are from OEMs who have excess. It is all grey market...not illegal, but not necessarily through authorized channels. On Kinguin you can pay around an extra dollar as a type of "insurance" in the event the code you buy doesn't work or gets deactivated. Also, Kinguin is sort of like Ebay in that anybody can sell stuff, but it's probably wise to buy from the "big" sellers with tons of positive feedback.

I'll give you a quick illustration of how I got Doom. Months ago I noticed that you could pre-order the game for ~$35 bucks or so on Amazon. I passed. I played the multiplayer and hated it. But a day or two before the game was released, I decided to buy it--but at that point you could only order it for full retail ($59). Since I hated the demo, I wasn't going to pay full retail for an unknown so I was going to wait for reviews and then a big sale. Then I remembered Kinguin--they had it for $32 with the Multiplayer DLC. I decided to grab it and paid the extra buck something for the insurance. When you're checking out, they offer you some discounts on other stuff..so I ended up grabbing 5 random Steam keys for something like $3 and opted out of the "insurance" for those. I got my 5 random Steam keys via the Kinguin website about 5 minutes after checking out (via PayPal). I got a message that I'd get my Steam code for Doom on release day. The codes for the random games worked fine...so well that I subsequently went back and purchased some more. I got my code for Doom the day before release, entered it in Steam, and it has worked 100% fine.

I've bought gray market goods regularly since the early 90s, but this is obviously digital. Any time you buy something from the gray market there's a chance you could be left hanging--but as long as you take that into account going in, you can save a ton of money. I'd also point out that Kinguin and other services like them are not fringe, pirate sites. They're pretty mainstream in the gaming world--they advertise and even sponsor big Twitch streamers. I still buy stuff directly on Steam and COG, but this is another option I consider if I'm interested in something but unwilling to pay the often inflated Steam prices.
